package_info.why_malicious: The 'everything' package is malicious because it intentionally declares dependencies on thousands of other npm packages in its package.json, creating an extreme transitive dependency chain. This results in denial of service (DoS) by exhausting system resources (disk space, CPU, network bandwidth) during installation, and disrupts the npm ecosystem by preventing the unpublishing of a vast number of packages due to dependency entanglement. The package was created as a disruptive prank, but its impact is harmful to users and the registry.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At install-time, the package.json declares dependencies on thousands of other npm packages, causing npm to recursively resolve, fetch, and install all of them, resulting in massive resource consumption and denial of service.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Declaring dependencies on thousands of packages is highly abnormal and serves no legitimate purpose. This pattern is designed to overwhelm the npm package manager and the user's system, causing installation to consume excessive resources.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages declare only the minimal set of dependencies required for their functionality. This package intentionally depends on nearly every public npm package, violating the principle of minimal, necessary dependencies and responsible ecosystem participation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: A legitimate meta-package might aggregate a set of related modules (e.g., a framework with plugins), but would never depend on thousands of unrelated packages or attempt to pull in the entire registry.
key_indicators: package.json with a dependency list numbering in the thousands
Dependency names follow a chunked or auto-generated pattern (e.g., @everything-registry/chunk-*)
No functional code present, only dependency declarations
Installation triggers massive network and disk activity

attack_chain.action: User installs the 'everything' package, triggering npm to resolve and install all declared dependencies.
attack_chain.leads_to: System resource exhaustion as npm attempts to download and install thousands of packages.

attack_chain.action: Transitive dependencies recursively pull in even more packages, amplifying the resource consumption.
attack_chain.leads_to: Denial of service (DoS) on the user's system and potential strain on the npm registry.

attack_chain.action: Due to npm's unpublishing policy, all packages depended on by 'everything' become locked and cannot be unpublished.
attack_chain.leads_to: Long-term disruption in the npm ecosystem, preventing package maintainers from removing their own packages.

behavioral_signatures: Packages with dependency lists numbering in the thousands
Meta-packages that depend on nearly all public npm packages
Install-time resource exhaustion (CPU, disk, network) without any functional code
file_indicators: package.json files with hundreds or thousands of dependencies
Dependency names following a chunked or auto-generated pattern (e.g., @everything-registry/chunk-*)
network_indicators: Massive spike in npm registry requests during install
Unusually high number of package downloads in a single install session
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages whose package.json declares an abnormally large number of dependencies (e.g., more than 100). Flag meta-packages that depend on broad swathes of the registry, especially those with auto-generated or chunked dependency names. Watch for install-time resource exhaustion or npm install sessions that attempt to download thousands of packages. Alert on packages that, if installed, would prevent unpublishing of a large number of other packages due to dependency entanglement.
